summary: DNSSEC normally secures even delegations to unsigned subzones, which can be costly for large zones. This experimental document describes an Opt-In model that lets administrators skip that cryptography for such delegations, reducing the cost of adopting DNSSEC. It defines an experimental protocol, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: If a school has thousands of empty lockers, this lets you skip putting locks on the empty ones so you can still protect the busy ones.

questions: how to reduce dnssec cost for large zones
what is an opt-in nsec record
subtitle: An experiment that lets big DNSSEC zones leave unsigned delegations out of the NSEC chain.

tldr.problem: In DNSSEC, delegations to unsigned subzones are still cryptographically secured. For large delegation-centric zones, or zones whose insecure delegations change rapidly, maintaining the NSEC record chain can be very costly.
tldr.mechanism: Opt-In lets a zone administrator remove insecure delegations from the NSEC chain. An NSEC record is tagged as Opt-In by leaving its NSEC bit unset in the type map, and such a record only covers insecure delegations in the span it defines.
tldr.outcome: Zones save space and avoid re-signing NSEC records when insecure delegations change, but resolvers lose the ability to prove that an insecure delegation in that span exists or does not. The RFC strongly recommends using Opt-In sparingly.

facts.label: Opt-In tag
facts.value: NSEC bit unset in the type map

today: RFC 4956 is an Experimental RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an experiment that interoperates with standard DNSSEC only through private algorithms.

sections.title: The Cost Opt-In Targets
sections.content:
In standard DNSSEC, a delegation to an unsigned subzone sits in a signed name with an NSEC record that proves the subzone has no DS record. For large delegation-centric zones, or zones where insecure delegations are updated rapidly, the cost of keeping that NSEC chain current can be extremely high compared with the gain of cryptographically proving that unsecured zones exist.

Using Opt-In, a zone administrator can choose to remove insecure delegations from the NSEC chain. The mechanism extends the meaning of the NSEC record by using a redundant bit in its type map.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking every empty locker costs a lot of time. Opt-In lets the school skip the empty ones.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Private Algorithms
sections.content:
This is an experimental extension to DNSSEC. To keep it from confusing ordinary validators, a zone using Opt-In must be signed only with private algorithm 253 aliases: 3.optin.verisignlabs.com for DNSSEC algorithm 3 (DSA) and 5.optin.verisignlabs.com for algorithm 5 (RSASHA1). Servers MUST NOT use any other algorithms for such zones.

Resolvers MUST NOT apply the Opt-In validation rules unless the zone is signed with one of these private algorithms. The experiment also relaxes the rule in RFC 4035 Section 5.4 that validators ignore the NSEC bit in the type map.
sections.plainLanguage: Opt-In zones wear a special badge so that normal DNSSEC checkers know to treat them as unsigned instead of getting confused.

sections.title: How Opt-In NSEC Records Work
sections.content:
A normal NSEC record has its own NSEC bit set in the type map. An Opt-In tagged NSEC record has that bit zero or unspecified. Because the bit only says the NSEC record itself exists, it is redundant and safe to use as a tag.

An Opt-In NSEC record does not assert the existence or non-existence of the delegations it covers, except one with the same name. Any name in the span MUST be an insecure delegation. It still asserts the existence or non-existence of other RRsets at its own owner name. A zone MAY mix Opt-In and standard NSEC records. If an NSEC record is not Opt-In, there MUST NOT be insecure delegations between it and its next name.

Because those delegations are not in the chain, they can be added or removed without recalculating or re-signing NSEC records.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag says: between here and the next entry there may be unlocked lockers, and I am not vouching for them.

sections.title: Server and Resolver Behavior
sections.content:
Servers. Signing tools MUST NOT produce zones that put anything but insecure delegations in an Opt-In span, and servers MUST refuse to load or serve such zones, including via AXFR or IXFR. When returning an Opt-In insecure delegation, a server MUST include the covering NSEC RRset in the Authority section, which may require searching for it because its owner name differs from the delegation. Servers MUST NOT process Dynamic Update requests against Opt-In zones and SHOULD answer with RCODE=REFUSED, because the rules for changing the chain are not defined.

Resolvers. Resolvers MUST be able to use Opt-In NSEC records to prove the insecure status of a referral and to validate negative answers to DS queries. Caching resolvers MUST be able to find the covering NSEC when returning referrals.

The AD bit MUST NOT be set on a Name Error response covered by an Opt-In NSEC, on an Opt-In insecure delegation response unless the NSEC owner name equals the delegation name, or on a NOERROR/NODATA response to a DS query unless the NSEC owner name matches the query name. In those cases not all data has been cryptographically verified.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers must never hide anything but empty lockers inside an unlocked stretch, and checkers must not say everything was verified when part of the answer was not.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs and Transition
sections.content:
Unsigned names are insecure by definition, so records with unsigned names have the same weaknesses as records in an unsigned zone. Records with signed names have the same security with or without Opt-In. The main change is losing the ability to prove that an insecure delegation exists or does not within an Opt-In span. An attacker may insert or delete such records, including replacing a wildcard expansion with a forged delegation, and a resolver would have to believe a forged referral. For that reason the RFC strongly RECOMMENDS using Opt-In sparingly, says zone signing tools SHOULD NOT default to it, and says they MAY choose not to support it at all.

Opt-In is not backwards compatible with standard DNSSEC. Every element between the validator and the authoritative server, including caching middleboxes, must understand the experiment for validation to work.
sections.plainLanguage: The price of skipping locks is that a trickster could slip a fake item into an unlocked locker and nobody could prove it was not there before.
